The post Digital foundations for a changing sector: a response to Sir Chris Husband’s New Choices essay appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Liam Earney, managing director for higher education and research at Jisc.

Professor Sir Chris Husbands’ new HEPI paper, New choices: Revisiting futures for higher education in England, offers an interesting assessment of where the sector is currently headed. It argues that English higher education is not moving towards a single, planned future, but instead is entering an unstable period of financial contraction, greater institutional differentiation, research concentration, changing student expectations and rapid technological disruption.

One of the central observations of the paper is its recognition that universities cannot respond to these pressures through another round of restructuring alone. Husbands draws an important distinction between measures intended to preserve an existing operating model and those designed to create a genuinely different one.

The sector is no stranger to change. Universities and sector bodies have spent years running transformation programmes, reorganising services and introducing new systems. Yet for all this activity, institutions have often changed their component parts without changing their underlying model. Cutting modules or closing courses may reduce cost, but it does not change how the institution fundamentally works. The challenge now is to develop the capability to operate differently.

A differentiated higher education system will require institutions to make choices about their mission, partnerships, and areas of strategic focus. Some may become part of larger regional groupings. Others may focus more sharply on teaching, specialist provision or particular areas of research. Many will need to collaborate more extensively, share services or build new relationships with further education providers, employers and local government.

None of this will happen through strategy documents alone. Institutional change depends on the underlying capacity and capability to redesign processes, connect services, and operate across organisational boundaries. Where systems are fragmented, data is unreliable and platforms cannot communicate, even straightforward reforms become slow, costly and risky. Anyone who has worked with student records systems will understand the challenge.

Digital foundations need to be understood as part of the sector’s change infrastructure. They include the less visible capabilities on which institutional adaptation depends, from trust and identity to reliable data and strong digital governance. These are not just technical issues; together they determine how effectively institutions respond to change.

The paper is especially persuasive when it argues that the sector is being pushed towards greater collaboration without the infrastructure needed to support it. Government may want more specialisation, regional coordination and institutional cooperation, but collaboration is difficult when universities operate incompatible systems, duplicated processes and different approaches to data and identity. A collaborative sector requires more than goodwill; it needs pragmatic mechanisms that allow institutions to work together.

That means creating practical mechanisms that allow institutions to work together while preserving their autonomy, whether through shared services or coordinated provision across higher and further education.

The Lifelong Learning Entitlement illustrates why this is important. Its success will depend not only on policy and funding, but also on institutions being able to support modular admissions, credit accumulation, transfer and recognition. Husbands explicitly identifies institutional systems development and digital badging as necessary parts of implementation.

The same principle applies to institutional consolidation. Mergers and shared-service arrangements may look attractive on paper, but they are difficult to deliver when organisations have incompatible data, contracts, platforms and security arrangements. Without planning for digital integration, structural change can create additional complexity rather than resilience.

The digital foundations in the sector need to be treated as an enabling condition of sector reform, not as a separate technology agenda.

AI will also have an impact on the futures highlighted in the paper. It is already reshaping the sector in a multitude of ways. But rather than just adopting tools, we must also look at the underlying infrastructure and governance needed to use them well. The paper notes that many institutions lack the digital foundations on which meaningful AI deployment depends. Legacy systems, fragmented data and limited investment capacity make it difficult to move at the pace of technological change.

Without stronger digital foundations, AI risks becoming another layer added to already complex institutions. It may automate existing processes without improving them, deepen dependence on external suppliers or amplify weaknesses in data and governance. However, with the right foundations, AI can become part of a broader programme of institutional redesign, supporting more flexible learning and more effective institutional operations.

The sector needs shared digital foundations that allow institutions to change in different ways while remaining connected, resilient and capable of collaboration.

For us at Jisc, we have a clear responsibility. We need to work with stakeholders across the sector to define the shared digital foundations a changing sector requires, identify where common approaches can reduce duplication and support institutions to adapt without losing control of their missions. Husbands’ paper makes clear that the old model cannot simply be restored. The sector is moving towards greater differentiation, collaboration and complexity. The question is whether that transition will be managed or just endured.

Digital foundations will be central to the answer.

title: ‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shock
summary:
Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation

“It was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust.

“I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved.

full_text:
“It was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust.

“I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved.

Her sudden upheaval was emblematic of the wider crisis in student housing. While UK universities face a financial crisis, providers of accommodation are grappling with falling international student numbers, a cost of living squeeze and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.

A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty.

It had been touted as the ultimate student living: smart city centre blocks with gyms, cinemas and rooftop terraces have sprung up across the UK. A world away from the traditional image of dirty and dingy shared digs, the flats have offered a spacious alternative for their relatively affluent residents – often international students. Now, some sit half empty, and several schemes have gone bust.

Sriwiboonrattan was among nearly 70 students in Dundee who were left scrambling to find accommodation in late July after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a 116-room city centre block that had a concierge and a shared games lounge with a pool table.

Despite the boom in housing developed by financial institutions in recent years, many students heading off to university this term faced a different dilemma. Rents at the tower blocks have grown much faster than maintenance loans for British students, leaving PSBAs financially out of reach.

Meanwhile, the cost of living crisis has put financial pressure on students seeking university-owned or managed accommodation, while rising rents have hit those wanting to live in shared private rentals. Underlining the scale of the shortage of affordable housing, the students’ union in Bristol included an emergency support number for the housing charity Shelter in an email to new students.

At PSBAs, the national average rent, excluding London, is £191 a week including bills, according to the website StuRents.

At the top end, en suite rooms in Manchester command a weekly rent of £170 to £320, whereas in London, en suite rooms are £250 to £650 a week, and studio apartments in Bloomsbury cost between £550 and £800 plus.

“I wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham,” says Soham Chougale, 23, a student at University College Birmingham. “I am an international student, so my working hours are capped at 20 hours [a week in term time], which means I can’t afford to live in PBSA,” says Chougale, the education officer at UCB Guild of Students.

He lived in university-owned dorms for the first two years of his aviation management degree and now shares a two-bedroom privately rented flat with a friend. On campus, he paid £660 rent including bills a month during the first year, which rose by 10% in his second year; now he pays £700 rent a month, excluding bills.

While living on campus “gave me the best feeling of community” and “I still have those friends that I met on the first day”, the wifi was patchy, some facilities were broken and there was a mouse infestation, he recounts.

“PBSA can be quite pricey,” says Matthew Pointon, a real estate analyst at Capital Economics, but adds: “Normally professionally managed buildings are better in terms of quality.”

In London, which attracts the richest students, there is still demand for upmarket accommodation, but outside the capital, there is an oversupply in some cities, such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham.

This week, university staff began strikes in Dundee, Edinburgh and Nottingham over budget cuts, with the industrial action threatening to wipe out a term of teaching for many students.

In Nottingham, demand has fallen from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, while 7,700 more PSBA beds came on to the market, the student housing charity Unipol calculated.

The number of students arriving from China has stagnated, and those from the new growth countries India, Pakistan and Nigeria are much more cost-conscious than the pre-Covid students from China, says Martin Blakey, an adviser on student living and the former chief executive of Unipol.

Deniz Yalçın, the chair of the Newington-Meadows branch of the Living Rent union in Edinburgh, says: “In Edinburgh, we’re seeing an explosion of PBSA despite the fact that this type of development is not needed and actually fuels the housing affordability crisis here.

“Many of them lie empty during most of the year, using the Fringe [festival] to bolster profits. Some have even been bought by the council to become temporary housing.”

Richard Ward, the head of research at StuRents, says the key issue is the big gap between maintenance loans and rents, after double-digit rental growth at PBSA blocks and shared houses in recent years.

Maintenance loans have declined in real terms because of below-inflation increases and frozen parental income thresholds. “And what have we seen? More students commuting,” Ward says. “Outside of London, you’re talking about £300 rent a week to make a new PBSA scheme viable. Well, your average British student is paying about £160 a week.”

Occupancy rates at the tower blocks range between 71.3% in Glasgow, 69.9% in Coventry, 89.7% in Bristol and 95.3% in Exeter, as of August, according to StuRents.

Student housing providers are increasingly focusing on the cities with the best universities. Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, has stepped up sales of unwanted sites.

The loss-making group aims to slim down its portfolio to 55,000-60,000 beds in 20 cities compared with 72,000 beds in 29 cities at present, “to increase alignment to the UK’s strongest universities, where student demand is robust and growing”. Unite reduced rents and tenancy lengths in Nottingham, Leicester and Sheffield, the “most challenging” cities, earlier this year, and rooms start from £99 a week in Coventry.

About 95% of new student beds are being built in cities with Russell Group universities, up from 81% last year, according to the property agency Knight Frank, by investors such as Blackstone, KKR and Greystar. The Russell Group is an association of 24 established UK universities including Cambridge, Oxford, Durham, Edinburgh, Manchester and King’s College London.

Smaller PBSA operators are struggling, with average occupancy levels of 85% across the sector, Unipol estimates. The housing association Sanctuary has been trying to sell student assets of more than 5,600 beds, across 21 properties in eight locations across the UK, for nearly two years, and in July said the buyer had “sought to revisit pricing assumptions” citing changes in economic and market conditions.

Investors poured £164m into the PBSA sector between April and June, one of the lowest quarterly levels on record, although total investment of £2.3bn in the first half was ahead of 2025, according to Knight Frank research. Only 13 deals were completed during the second quarter.

In response to the sector’s headwinds, several PBSA owners plan to rent some floors to young professionals, while one block in Leeds that is only 50% full could partly be used for short-term hotel stays.

In Dundee, Sriwiboonrattan has found alternative accommodation – a studio in the nearby Parklands block – which has a sky lounge with city views, gym and rooftop terrace – where she is paying weekly rent of £240, with financial support from her family. At Marketgait, she says the “walls were thin” with noise coming in from neighbours and lifts unreliable, so she prefers her new surroundings now the initial shock has dissipated.

Others still face a bleak picture, with the freshers’ week parties fading into the memory and the academic year now in full swing. Lewis Wilson, the vice-president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says: “The whole system is broken around student finance and student loans. Some students are going homeless, some students are relying on food banks.” A quarter of student unions now provide a food bank or food pantry.

Wilson, who graduated from the University of Sussex two years ago with a law degree, argues that PBSAs need to be better regulated, and become more affordable. “For the students on lower incomes like I was, I would never have been able to afford a PBSA,” he says.

The government says: “We expect higher education providers to consider the supply, and affordability of student accommodation in relation to their anticipated student intakes and across all years of study at least five years ahead.

“Recognising the inherent uncertainties in student demand and housing delivery timelines, providers should engage with the local planning authority on need.”

title: From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schools
summary:
Ten years after full extent of problem was revealed, Guardian investigation finds schools facing uphill battle amid rapid societal changes

  • Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales

It is 10 years since a report first revealed the epic scale of sexual bullying, harassment and abuse girls faced in England’s schools on a daily basis.

The report, by MPs on the women and equalities committee, showed the horrifying normality of child-on-child abuse in schools. The need for government action was “overwhelming”, said the committee chair, Maria Miller. Ofsted duly investigated, recommendations were written, promises were made and a new sex education curriculum was rolled out.

full_text:
It is 10 years since a report first revealed the epic scale of sexual bullying, harassment and abuse girls faced in England’s schools on a daily basis.

The report, by MPs on the women and equalities committee, showed the horrifying normality of child-on-child abuse in schools. The need for government action was “overwhelming”, said the committee chair, Maria Miller. Ofsted duly investigated, recommendations were written, promises were made and a new sex education curriculum was rolled out.

A decade later, and six years after the Everyone’s Invited movement began to collect anonymous testimonies from victims, a Guardian investigation has shown the problem persists unabated at schools in England and Wales. In many ways it may be more pernicious as a result of the rise of social media, misogyny and the mass consumption of online pornography by teenage boys.

The freedom of information investigation captures only the most serious incidents; those reported to and recorded by police. Interviews with experts, lawyers and campaigners suggest many more cases never get reported, often because the children involved are under the age of criminal responsibility and the assault is dismissed as “age-related exploration”.

Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors and a specialist in abuse claims, has dealt with cases of child-on-child sexual abuse in private and state schools, inner-city schools, rural schools, primary, secondary and boarding schools for more than a decade. He says the impact on victims can endure for years and many suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.

“From my own cases I can see it’s happening up and down the country to children of all ages,” he said. In many instances, however, schools were still struggling to deal with it appropriately. “If you have children in a physical fight, schools know exactly how to react. When you are talking about sexual assault, it’s a different matter.”

Lord is currently representing a secondary school pupil who reported being subjected to a number of sexual and physical assaults by fellow pupils in a changing room. The family is seeking a claim for negligence and breach of human rights against the school for its failure to protect the child.

“Schools do have a duty to ensure that both children [involved in an incident] receive their education, but I am aware of situations where the children continue at the same school and the victim has felt that they have not received adequate support to enable them to engage safely with their studies after disclosing incidents of sexual violence.

“Victims can find themselves being ostracised, which may represent a breach of the Human Rights Act,” he added.

Lord also represents a number of primary school children, including a boy who reported being seriously sexually assaulted by another child on school premises. He was scared he would be hit if he did not comply.

“The biggest issue for me with primary-age cases, when children are below the age of criminal responsibility, is there is often no real statutory investigation and there’s an overreliance on ‘age-related exploration’.”

What typically happens on primary school premises, Lord said, is that a child is taken to a more hidden area by fellow pupils – behind a shed, climbing frame or bushes – is forced to undress and is assaulted, often under threat of being excluded from play and friendship groups.

While most victims of sexual abuse in schools are girls, boys are also targeted. Bethany’s* eight-year-old son was sexually abused on three occasions by a classmate during play dates at her home.

She only discovered what had happened when he began crying at bedtime. She reported it to the school but claims it tried to dismiss what happened as relationship difficulties. “This was not a relationship difficulty. This was sexual assault,” she said. “No one was taking it seriously.”

Her son was never interviewed. There was no proper investigation into what happened and no appropriate safety plan was drawn up to protect her son. “They wanted to sweep it all under the carpet, and that’s not good enough. It was like he was not believed.” In the end, he moved to another school. The other boy remained.

“My son was never treated as a victim in any sense. They offered him no real support. What was worse than the incident itself was how the school dealt with it. It was just appalling. We both felt very, very let down,” said Bethany.

Richard Scorer is another lawyer who deals with civil claims arising from sexual abuse and receives regular approaches from parents, and in some cases teenagers who have suffered child-on-child sexual abuse of various kinds in school.

“We see a lot more of it now than we would have done even a few years ago. As well as a greater awareness, it’s also possible there’s a greater underlying level of abuse and that may have something to do with the pervasiveness of online pornography, particularly in the lives of teenage boys.

“It’s the full range of sexual assault, ranging from unwanted touching to rape. Some of that will take place on school premises, some of it will be off-site. Boys are overwhelmingly the perpetrators. There’s obviously all of the issues around revenge porn and the sharing of intimate photographs – that’s a big issue as well.

“My sense is that schools in some instances are struggling to know how to respond because of the extent of what’s going on and because safeguarding is quite resource intensive. Schools are forced into a bit of a social work role, picking up the pieces from things that are going wrong in society at large.”

Tony Hartney, a school improvement consultant and former headteacher, said awareness around child-on-child sexual abuse was much better in schools and there was a greater willingness to tackle such issues, but they remained “tricky” to handle.

“When there are allegations made like this, schools are very sensitive to the needs of both young people involved to try and make it as viable as possible for them to continue with their education in schools.

“The difficulty of course is things take time. Whilst investigations are going on, you ideally want them to be in schools and to have as normal an education as they can. It’s tricky for schools to manage these situations.”

When she became children’s commissioner for England in 2021, Rachel de Souza knew from her time as a headteacher about sexual harassment and abuse in schools.

“But what I heard as I listened to young people shocked me. Children were viewing violent pornography, it was changing behaviour and peer-on-peer abuse was widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet.

“We have taken important steps in the last few years – from work to bring highly skilled professionals together under one roof to care for child victims of abuse, to action to prevent children from accessing pornography, and a focus on evidence-based relationships education that addresses the realities of teenagers’ lives.

“But as these figures show, we have a long way to go. This is not simply a school or college issue, it is a societal one. We need to address the causes – harmful sexual behaviours are increasingly shaped by the content and cultures that children are exposed to online.

“And we need to urgently improve what happens when young victims of sexual assault speak out and their experience of the justice system, and make sure they get the support they need.”

* Name has been changed for reasons of anonymity

title: More than 1,200 Colorado students have earned a climate ‘seal’: ‘We’re the ones growing up in this world’
summary:
A statewide initiative pairs climate-focused coursework with community service – and is spreading to other states

As a student at a high school not far from Denver’s main airport, Anthony Muñoz wondered whether the jet fuel from airplanes flying above his campus was harming living things.

An avid gardener, Muñoz partnered with a local university to create a garden on the campus of his charter school, Vista Academy, filling it with native plants that could detect ground-level ozone pollution. He also worked with climate scientists from the National Center for Atmospheric Research, a federal office in nearby Boulder, who directed Muñoz on what data to collect, what the condition of leaves reveals about air quality and why milkweed matters for monarch butterfly migration.

full_text:
As a student at a high school not far from Denver’s main airport, Anthony Muñoz wondered whether the jet fuel from airplanes flying above his campus was harming living things.

An avid gardener, Muñoz partnered with a local university to create a garden on the campus of his charter school, Vista Academy, filling it with native plants that could detect ground-level ozone pollution. He also worked with climate scientists from the National Center for Atmospheric Research, a federal office in nearby Boulder, who directed Muñoz on what data to collect, what the condition of leaves reveals about air quality and why milkweed matters for monarch butterfly migration.

“One garden’s a very good data source,” said Muñoz. “Colorado’s so beautiful, and I would hate to see it wilt away.”

Muñoz built the “ozone garden” for his capstone project as part of Colorado’s seal of climate literacy, a statewide initiative that pairs climate-focused coursework with hands-on community service. To earn the seal – an endorsement on high school diplomas and transcripts – students must complete at least two advanced courses that cover the Earth’s climate systems and an approved project that tackles a climate issue in their community.

Since 2024, when Colorado lawmakers approved the seal, 26 of the state’s 179 school districts have adopted it, according to Lyra Colorado, an education non-profit that advocates for the seal. Now, the model is spreading to other states. Maine adopted its own climate seal earlier this year, and California just signed into law a bill to establish the seal for graduates there. Youth coalitions have pushed for the policy in Hawaii and Minnesota, with varying success.

Proponents of the seal argue that young people must understand and combat the climate crisis, without waiting for political leaders to reach consensus on how it should be taught. They also hope the endorsement will connect students to a rapidly expanding green workforce, preparing them to work on solar grids and climate-resilient farms or in water resource management and urban heat mitigation. And, as climate change begins to alter almost every aspect of human life, the seal could offer anxious teenagers a sense of agency and ability to make some difference.

“Where we can make the most difference is often in our local community,” said Laura Schifter, a senior fellow with the Aspen Institute’s This Is Planet Ed, a climate education group. She said the seal offers students a chance to learn about the climate crisis, a topic rarely covered in depth in K-12 classrooms, and called it “a really promising policy”.

Still, the seal has faced hurdles, including tight school district budgets, concern about new burdens on schools and the federal government’s attempts to refute climate science.

The idea for the seal originated with Lyra Colorado, the non-profit in Denver that supports community-based education programs. Rural students and educators the group was working with on another climate-related project said they wanted a way to explore climate change as a reality in their daily lives, not just through a dense unit in a textbook, according to Mary Seawell, Lyra’s CEO.

To earn the seal, students need to complete two classes that promote “climate literacy”, or basic principles of the climate crisis, such as its causes and how to mitigate it. One of them must be a science class, such as environmental studies, biology or earth science. The other course can be in any discipline, including the humanities or fine arts. For example, this year Denver public schools will build lessons about climate change into its state-mandated civics course, Seawell said. Student projects for the seal have addressed beaver dams, building trails, snow science and forestry management.

An estimated 1,200 students have received the seal so far, said Seawell.

Funding, though, has been a challenge: state lawmakers provided less than $20,000 for the seal’s rollout. Many students fund their projects out of pocket or, like Muñoz, secure grants: he co-wrote a $1m grant proposal to the city to pay for the gardens at his school. Lyra created its own grant program to help local schools pay for teachers’ time, student projects and even graduation cords.

Muñoz, now a sophomore studying mechanical engineering at the Colorado School of Mines, said the seal allowed him to learn climate leadership skills. He’s currently vice-president of the college’s environmental club and tries to inspire his peers to take action.

“Are you going to think beyond yourself and help not only those in need but the environment, or will you sit back and wait for someone else to change the world for you?” he said.

Getting more students involved in climate action

As more students like Muñoz graduate with the seal, many have started to work on climate issues at their colleges and in new states.

Rylan Neumann graduated last year from the Boulder Valley school district, enrolling that fall at the University of California, Berkeley, to study environmental economics. Almost immediately, she joined an eco-club and boarded a train to Sacramento, where she lobbied state lawmakers in support of the state’s pending climate seal bill.

“Getting more students involved in climate action and how they’ll be impacted in the future is essential,” she said. “We’re the ones growing up in this world.”

In Hawaii, a student member of the state board of education championed the endorsement for high schools on the islands. The Minnesota Youth Council, a state advisory board with representatives from middle and high schools, recommended the seal during this year’s legislative session.

State education officials in Maine, meanwhile, adopted the seal directly to avoid legislative debate.

“Students want to be involved in climate action, in environmental literacy, in green careers,” said Teddy Lyman, a K-12 climate education specialist in Maine. “They’re often doing the work already but don’t have the recognition. They didn’t see a sort of pathway to continue that work and embark on that as a potential career.”

During a spring pilot across nine high schools, Lyman expected roughly a dozen students to apply for the seal. Instead, he said, nearly 57 seniors did.

Melissa Luetje teaches science at Freeport high school, which enrolls about 600 students near Casco Bay. Warming and rising sea levels have eroded coastal infrastructure and flooded surface streets.

For a seal-approved class she teaches on research, students will monitor woodlands for insect damage, develop new ways to compost or commodify an invasive crab species, and work on a sustainable fishery.

“How climate impacts the coastal community is very different from the interior or a city,” Luetje said. “It’s up to each community to figure out what they value and how they want to roll this out.”

As the seal expands, proponents have tried to connect the high school endorsement directly to green workforce pipelines.

Lyra Colorado has started working with higher education institutions like Colorado Mountain College to align it with certification in the skilled trades, such as heat pump installation, solar grid maintenance or sustainable agriculture. She hopes universities will offer a partial minor or a course credit for incoming students who have the climate endorsement.

At the same time, Donald Trump has attacked the climate crisis as a “hoax”, and new federal scrutiny of renewable energy projects threatens philanthropic support for such initiatives. The treasury department and Republicans in Congress have targeted the tax-exempt status of non-profits that support climate causes, which Seawell said created a noticeable chilling effect among potential donors.

“Funders are worried,” she said.

The Trump administration has also tried to pull funding from and dismantle the National Center for Atmospheric Research, the climate research center that helped Muñoz with his school garden. He called the proposed cuts “devastating”.

Still, Muñoz, who plans to pursue biomedicine and one day become a professor, remains focused on climate issues.

He met virtually with students pushing for the seal in Minnesota. And he spent his first college break back at Vista Academy, assisting younger kids in the garden. They recently put the final touches on an elevated box designed for gardeners in wheelchairs.

And he’s writing code to make it easier for Vista students to continue collecting data in the ozone garden – even if it’s not clear when, or whether, NCAR scientists will get to use the data.

title: OPINION: Higher education has a trust problem, and families are right to demand transparency and candor
summary:
This opinion piece is the first in a series on trust and transparency in higher education.  Higher education runs on trust. A family commits four years and a significant sum of money on faith that the credential earned will hold value, that the institution has their student’s interests at heart and that the promises made […]

The post OPINION: Higher education has a trust problem, and families are right to demand transparency and candor appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
This opinion piece is the first in a series on trust and transparency in higher education.

Higher education runs on trust. A family commits four years and a significant sum of money on faith that the credential earned will hold value, that the institution has their student’s interests at heart and that the promises made during admissions will hold up long after enrollment.

That foundation of trust is getting harder to maintain.

A college can no longer count on being the only voice explaining its value. Prospective students can find firsthand student perspectives and check public data on cost and outcomes. The question for colleges is no longer simply what they say about themselves, but whether that account holds up when families look elsewhere.

Schools that once controlled their own narratives now compete with thousands of data points they didn’t create and can’t manage. The institutions that earn trust in this environment will be the ones willing to show what they deliver and build the systems that can prove it. Marketing alone won’t carry that weight anymore.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Most institutions are transparent about the front end of the student experience and far less transparent about the back end. Admissions pages are detailed. Program pages spell out courses and faculty. What happens after enrollment, especially after graduation, gets much less light.

That asymmetry reflects what institutions have historically been asked to measure. Accreditors and state agencies focus on completion rates and first-year placement. Marketing teams focus on what drives enrollment.

This is a trust problem wearing a data problem’s clothes. A family can’t evaluate a claim an institution is unwilling or unable to back up. When an institution says its program leads to strong career outcomes, that claim is only as credible as the evidence behind it. Building the connective institutional systems to show that evidence openly and consistently is how colleges can keep a family’s confidence after enrollment, not just before it.

Transparency isn’t just a content problem. It requires an institution to know things about itself that most don’t currently track: where graduates land three to five years out, and whether their credentials changed their trajectories. Income growth and career mobility show up on that timeline, not the day after commencement.

Institutions can bridge this knowledge gap by auditing postgraduation tracking systems, publishing multiyear career data and connecting admissions, career services and alumni networks. By moving beyond selective success stories, colleges and universities can deliver verified, actionable transparency for every student.

Related: I’m a college president, and I think colleges have to do a better job of controlling costs

Collecting such data is only the first step. The harder part is sharing it — even when it isn’t flattering. Publishing only the flattering numbers is a marketing exercise dressed up as transparency.

Genuine transparency means showing families results they can compare across schools and explaining the limits of that data. Publicly available, consistently defined data gives people a way to check institutional claims; context helps them understand what those numbers actually say.

The trust relationship between institutions, students and families too often ends at graduation. Alumni relations and career services usually run on separate tracks, and continuing education often sits apart from both.

A graduate looking for support five years into their career is unlikely to find a clear path through that structure, and that disconnect sends its own message about how far the institution’s promises were meant to reach.

Related: Use The Hechinger Report’s financial health tracker

Maintaining relationships with alumni and tracking their professional progression provide higher education institutions with solid evidence to demonstrate the lasting worth of their degrees. That ongoing engagement takes shape when universities establish clear routes for stackable qualifications as industries transform and when they build employer networks that offer verifiable proof of student outcomes.

Community colleges and regional universities often have an edge here. Their proximity to local employers gives them direct visibility into whether graduates keep advancing in their careers, not simply whether they got hired — helping those institutions answer the core cost and career outcome questions prospective students are increasingly asking.

An institution that lacks the systems to back its claims with evidence loses the benefit of the doubt it used to get by default.

Brand strength alone (historic prestige and name recognition) won’t be what sets institutions apart over the next decade. Having the right systems to track student outcomes will.

That starts with breaking down data silos so that student outcome data moves freely across the offices that use it instead of staying locked in whichever one gathered it first.

Accountability to graduates has to survive well past the day tuition is paid.

Building institutional systems that hold up to scrutiny is a higher bar than most institutions set for themselves today. It’s also the only foundation that will hold as families keep asking sharper questions.

Stephen Green is the chief partnerships officer at Noodle, where he oversees all of Noodle’s university partnerships focusing on their evolving needs and growth, along with Noodle’s corporate marketing efforts.

title: As more colleges close, advocates are calling for them to be turned into housing
summary:
QUINCY, Mass. — Waist-high weeds climb through cracks in the tennis courts. Ivy snakes across the locked-shut entrance of a redbrick former women’s dormitory.  Canada geese graze on the baseball field. Wild turkeys scratch in the underbrush. The post As more colleges close, advocates are calling for them to be turned into housing appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
QUINCY, Mass. — Waist-high weeds climb through cracks in the tennis courts. Ivy snakes across the locked-shut entrance of a redbrick former women’s dormitory.

Canada geese graze on the baseball field. Wild turkeys scratch in the underbrush.

Nature is reclaiming what remains of Eastern Nazarene College, which closed last year after its enrollment plummeted and its liabilities ballooned to an unsustainable $18 million.

It’s one among a growing number of closed colleges sitting empty, some for years stretching into decades, as communities fight over what they should become and trustees struggle to pay off creditors.

All of this is happening as the country faces an urgent need for a resource that a mounting number of experts say should be built on abandoned campuses like this one: housing.

Converting closed campuses into badly needed housing is a timely way of using one problem to solve another, these experts say.

Many neighbors think so, too.

“I don’t want to see it wasted,” said Donna Glynn, a teacher who has lived for 50 years across the street from Eastern Nazarene, in this city of about 100,000 just south of Boston. “We could have nice, new, clean housing.”

Efforts to reuse the campus for that purpose have taken so many twists and turns, however, that Glynn choked up as she recounted them. And the former college remains unused.

“Why would you throw this resource away?” she asked, nodding toward the former college.

The United States needs to build about 3.7 million homes to meet demand, according to the mortgage company Freddie Mac. Massachusetts will have to add at least 222,000 by 2035, state officials estimate. Quincy alone is short 4,400 homes, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the think tank the American Enterprise Institute found.

Eastern Nazarene seems a perfect place to build some. It’s in a residential neighborhood and close to public transportation. Before it held its last commencement, it reached an agreement to be acquired by a private equity and development company owned by an alumnus who reportedly planned to put more than 600 units of housing on the 27-acre site.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

But Quincy’s mayor said that number of units was too high, and — after the deal fell through — proposed that the city itself buy the campus for about $23 million and redevelop it with fewer homes than the developer proposed. Then the city council rejected that idea in June as too expensive.

The debate has become contentious and political, and no one involved would respond to requests to discuss it — the developer, the mayor, the three city councilors who voted for his plan, the college’s transition board or its real estate attorney.

“It seems an easy case to make” to transform closed college campuses into housing, said Christian Koulichkov, director of real estate brokerage of the financial services company Hilco Global, who noted he was not speaking specifically about Eastern Nazarene or Quincy. “It makes sense just from a need perspective. The one commodity we have too little of in this country is housing, and affordable housing to boot.”

It isn’t easy to transform college campuses into housing. They’re often not zoned for it. Many colleges that have closed weren’t taken care of at the end. Their buildings are old. They don’t meet accessibility standards. Dorms have shared bathrooms and crowded layouts that are hard to reconfigure into fully functional apartments.

Even as the college closing crisis speeds up — with 442 private, nonprofit colleges and universities at risk of closing or having to merge over the next 10 years, according to a new estimate from Huron Consulting Group — few governing boards have planned ahead for the possibility that their institutions might shut down. And communities seldom think it will happen to them, so do little to prepare for handling a suddenly vacant campus.

That’s what Kurt Wheeler, the mayor of Cazenovia, New York, found when 200-year-old Cazenovia College defaulted on $25 million in debt and closed in 2023, leaving an empty collection of land and buildings in the heart of his village.

When officials looked around to see how other places in the same situation were repurposing their closed colleges, “We could not find a successful example, especially in small towns,” said Wheeler. “So we said, ‘We’re going to be the first.’ Because this problem is not going to go away.”

The village conducted a feasibility study and changed the zoning for the property to make it more attractive to developers; a group of local investors then bought up many of the buildings to convert them into a new “town square,” with housing and other uses.

“If we don’t want this really awful outcome of the weeds and the falling-apart buildings, we all have to be a little bit flexible,” Wheeler said.

Related: More than a quarter of private colleges are at risk of closing, new projection shows

Many other communities with closed colleges, however, continue to be stuck with weeds and falling-apart buildings.

“Field of weeds,” the local newspaper called the empty campus of Limestone University in South Carolina, which closed last year under $38 million of debt and has been mired in a dispute among its creditors, a lawsuit from former employees seeking back pay and demands from former students for refunds for classes that were never taught.

Virginia Intermont College has sat vacant for 12 years, even after a Chinese company bought it. Four of its buildings burned down in a huge fire in 2024 and the rubble still hasn’t been cleared, while many of the remaining structures have been vandalized.

Redevelopment efforts are sometimes held up by neighbors, who also want a say in what happens to campuses.

“Save our Neighborhood” read red signs on front lawns all around the former Eastern Nazarene. They were put there by opponents of the original high-density development plan.

“I’d love to keep it as it is” — as a quiet and pastoral enclave — said Lauren Hickey, who walks her dog, Charlee, on the campus, shaded by trees so exotic it’s been designated as an arboretum named for a former botany professor.

Related: Pace of college closings picks up, with more projected

Some communities have managed to move ahead with housing on closed college campuses, however.

A developer plans to build 165 homes on the 60-acre former campus of Holy Names University in Oakland, California, which closed in 2023, for instance. A nonprofit is putting dozens of apartments for former foster youth on the campus of the former Dana College near Omaha, which closed in 2010, and has also proposed senior housing there.

Low-cost apartments have been built on a closed branch campus in Denver of Johnson & Wales University. And about 160 units of high-end senior housing have replaced part of the former Newbury College campus near Boston.

Conversions into housing also are proposed for more recently closed college campuses.

Alumni, neighbors and local nonprofit organizations have formed a partnership to build affordable housing in western Massachusetts on the 275-acre former Simon’s Rock campus of Bard College, which the college shed last year. Officials in the community surrounding Trinity Christian College near Chicago, which closed in the spring, are encouraging the organization that bought it to sell off parts of the campus for senior housing.

Related: Business, government and education leaders try to reinvent college from scratch

Senior housing and homes are planned for closed branch campuses of the University of Wisconsin in Fond du Lac and Waukesha. And a nonprofit community trust is negotiating to buy the former Sterling College in Vermont, which closed in the spring, and make it into housing, among other uses.

Many of these aspirations are likely to take patience, said Chris Ales, a real estate developer who is transforming several buildings into housing at Iowa Wesleyan University, which closed in 2023. But “it’s a good solution, despite the challenges. A lot of college campuses are well-suited in their footprint for an adaptive reuse into apartments.”

The kind of senior housing being built on many former campuses, including his, frees up other homes for younger buyers, Ales said. And most of a campus’s original green space remains, “so that is usually a positive for the neighbors” who — as at Eastern Nazarene — are accustomed to enjoying it.

None of this makes the process of replacing colleges with housing any easier, he noted.

Still, Ales said, “I’ve stood before many a city council” that was skeptical about transforming college campuses for that purpose. “And in the end, you get where you need to be. Because it’s common sense.”

Contact writer Jon Marcus at 212-678-7556, jmarcus@hechingerreport.org or jpm.82 on Signal.

title: Despair over future fuels political anxiety for college students on the cusp of adulthood
summary: Their anxiety is fueling a restlessness with a national political system that they worry is no longer capable of improving their lives or no longer interested in helping.
full_text:
EAST LANSING, Mich. (AP) — Frankie Llerandi, 21, has been unable to land a single internship in his three years at Michigan State University.

He will graduate in the spring with an economics degree and an interest in data analytics, but true adulthood seems maddeningly far away. Most of his cousins have not been able to buy a house or start a family deep into their 30s.

Kira Saiti, a 19-year-old sophomore, is more upset about the broader world than her own future. Every time she looks at her phone she sees images of violence and horror, both in the Middle East and closer to home.

"It's kind of hard to look at that and say, 'This world is a great place,'" she said.

READ MORE: Some states are helping graduate students pay for school. Here's what borrowers should know

Julian Bautista, 20, saw his chosen profession of environmental work decimated by Trump administration cuts, pushing the junior to decide he will leave the United States to find work in the Netherlands when he graduates. He considers what remains his home country for the next 18 months to be a failure of democracy led by what he sees as corrupt politicians.

"Throughout my life, we've either stagnated or declined, we haven't improved," Bautista said.

For many of their classmates on campus and elsewhere around the country, the present looks bleak and the future uncertain at best. Their anxiety is fueling a restlessness with a national political system that they worry is no longer capable of improving their lives or no longer interested in helping.

Two years ago, grim economic vibes helped Donald Trump win a far larger share of young voters than is typical for a Republican — 47%, according to AP VoteCast, an extensive survey of the electorate. Now, anxiety about artificial intelligence and the Iran war has been added to the mix, powering a wave of disruptive candidates on the opposite end of the political spectrum who have been embraced by college students.

Llerandi, Saiti and Bautista all support a slate of progressive, antiestablishment Democratic candidates in Michigan who are pledging to shake up the status quo. Among them are Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official running for U.S. Senate, and Will Lawrence, a liberal activist trying to unseat Tom Barrett, the Republican congressman who represents the swing district that includes the university.

The future looks bleak for many students

Anxieties about the job market, homeownership and adulthood are widespread across the campus, even among those who are not deeply involved in politics.

"It's just something to laugh at, but, you know, I really do want a house when I'm older," said Praveen Amunugama, a 21-year-old biochemistry major who plans to go to graduate school in hopes the job market improves over the next two years.

His friends feel the same way.

"They want to be able to afford things, raise a good family," he said.

Despite the economic angst among young people, at first blush the picture does not look that bad for them. The unemployment rate for those age 22 to 27 is 7.2%, higher than the broader rate of 4.1% but lower than some other moments of economic calm.

A 2024 study found members of the younger generation known as Generation Z are poised to be wealthier than millennials, who themselves are wealthier than the prior generation despite the persistent sense of economic doom that accompanied their entry into the job market during the Great Recession.

Kevin Corinth, the economist who co-authored that study, said he understands Gen Z angst, given modern uncertainties, especially the prospect of AI reshaping various industries and data showing younger people are taking longer to leave home and start families.

"For previous generations, if you took certain paths you were likely to succeed, to do better than your parents," said Corinth, who is at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right think tank. For young people now, he acknowledged, that path is not as clear.

WATCH: Degree in three: Why more colleges are speeding up graduation timelines

Kathryn Edwards, a Texas-based economist, noted that unemployment among recent college graduates is at 5.6%, higher than at most other times in recent history other than the Great Recession. Combined with historically high housing prices and rising costs for essentials such as food and healthcare, that is a challenging environment for young people.

"It's pretty bad for them," Edwards said, adding that young people are picking up on broader warning signs in the economy. "So many aspects of our current economy, I think young people have gotten right."

They are also fully exposed to the new form of job hunting: AI-powered, digital and done almost exclusively online, where it is hard to discern real job openings from fake ones.

"Think about the amount they get spammed and scammed, and there are tons of fake jobs out there," said Marla McGraw, assistant dean of career management in Michigan State's business school. "They're always coming in here going, 'Is this real?'"

She spends a lot of time trying to buck up disenchanted students.

"Our message right now is the job market is tough, but you're tougher," McGraw said.

Students say political leaders are falling short

Young Americans' optimism about the job market has plummeted since 2024 and the gap between their view of the economy and those of their elders is greater than almost anywhere in the world, according to a Gallup survey earlier this year.

They are less likely to be engaged in politics and less likely to think it is important to vote, an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll found. They also are less likely to be concerned about political violence.

That dissolution of beliefs in traditional political values worries Karlee VanAntwerp.

The 21-year-old Michigan State senior is also head of the local chapter of Turning Point, the group for young conservatives whose founder, Charlie Kirk, was assassinated last year. VanAntwerp has been horrified to see Kirk's killing repeatedly, and sometimes menacingly, mocked online.

"Gen Z tends to be more extreme with their views," VanAntwerp said. "It makes it hard to work with people of different political beliefs, because even if you're in the middle, they assume you're crazy."

WATCH: Students question value of college as costs rise and AI reshapes jobs

VanAntwerp sees that feeding into the despair many of her generation feel about real change ever happening.

"One administration does a bunch of stuff, another administration comes in and wipes it all out," said VanAntwerp, who is also working for Barrett's campaign. "It feels like we always go in circles. That contributes to the political temperature being so high, because people feel nothing changes."

Her politics are the polar opposite of many liberal students who gathered to hear Lawrence, Barrett's Democratic challenger, talk in a classroom one recent evening, but there was a similar desire for dramatic change. Lawrence sympathized with the glum feelings of early adulthood and urged the students not to succumb to despair.

"When I was a little younger I wanted to drop out of society, and it was organizing that gave me a path in life," Lawrence said.

After the candidate left, however, Bautista still sounded on the verge of despair. He talked about how online influencers he trusts deride Democrats such as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York as "mini-mes" because, Bautista contended, they are just watered-down versions of Trump.

"Our leaders are representing us less," Bautista said. "People are desperate for big stuff."

title: Teaching Cyber Threats Differently: An AI-Powered Gamified Approach
summary:
While many academics are still locked in debate about whether to allow artificial intelligence in the classroom — fearing academic dishonesty, over-reliance, or loss of rigor — I made a deliberate choice to do the opposite. I brought AI in, put it at the center of the assessment, and asked my students to challenge it.  […]

The post Teaching Cyber Threats Differently: An AI-Powered Gamified Approach appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
While many academics are still locked in debate about whether to allow artificial intelligence in the classroom — fearing academic dishonesty, over-reliance, or loss of rigor — I made a deliberate choice to do the opposite. I brought AI in, put it at the center of the assessment, and asked my students to challenge it.

That decision was not taken lightly. The dilemma is real: AI tools can write essays, solve problems, and generate code with startling fluency. For many educators, this feels like a threat to the integrity of learning. But in a cybersecurity classroom, I saw a different possibility. What if AI were not the shortcut we feared, but the instrument through which students developed sharper, more critical thinking?

At Majan University College, I ventured where many colleagues hesitated — and the results reshaped how I teach cyber threats entirely.

The Dilemma Most Academics Face

The debate around AI in higher education is genuine and ongoing. Concerns about academic integrity are legitimate. When a student can paste an assignment question into ChatGPT and receive a polished response in seconds, the traditional essay or report begins to feel obsolete as an assessment instrument. Many institutions have responded with blanket bans or AI-detection policies.

But in a field like cybersecurity — where AI tools are already embedded in professional practice — banning them from the classroom risks producing graduates who are technically unprepared for the workplace. The question I kept returning to was not whether to allow AI, but how to design learning around it so that critical thinking remained non-negotiable.

“The question was not whether to allow AI, but how to design learning around it so that critical thinking remained non-negotiable.”

The Problem with Traditional Cybersecurity Instruction

Cybersecurity changes faster than most curricula can keep up with. Threat actors adapt weekly, new vulnerabilities emerge daily, and students are expected to master concepts ranging from network intrusion to social engineering — often in a single module. Lecture-based instruction struggles to keep pace.

In my own classroom, I noticed a recurring pattern: students could recite definitions of common vulnerabilities but froze when asked to identify them in a live network scenario. The knowledge was there — the application was not. I needed a method that built not just understanding, but instinct.

Step 1: Real Tools, Real Vulnerabilities

The first shift was putting industry-grade tools directly in students’ hands. Through a free licence from Tenable, students registered for and used Nessus Essentials — the same vulnerability scanner used by professional penetration testers — to scan their own lab environments and identify real weaknesses.

This was not a simulation. Students discovered actual vulnerabilities in their own machines: open ports, misconfigured services, outdated software with known exploits. The moment a student sees Nessus flag a critical-severity bind shell backdoor on their own system, the abstract becomes concrete. Cybersecurity stops being a theory module and starts feeling like a professional responsibility.

Figure 1 — Topic 7: Network Traffic Monitoring on MOVE (Majan E-Learning), showing Nessus Essentials registration, microlearning certificate upload, and the AI tools forum activity.

Step 2: Compare Three AI Tools, Then Decide

Once students identified a vulnerability, the next task was not to fix it immediately. Instead, they were asked to consult three AI tools of their choice — such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude AI — and compare the remediation approaches each one suggested. They then had to evaluate which solution was most technically sound, justify their choice, and document their reasoning in a forum post.

This comparative exercise produced some of the richest academic discussion I have seen in a computing module. Students quickly discovered that different AI tools gave meaningfully different answers — not just in wording, but in technical depth, persistence, and correctness. One student’s analysis of a critical bind shell backdoor (CVE-linked, severity 10.0) illustrated this perfectly.

Figure 2 — A student’s submitted report comparing Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini remediation approaches for a critical bind shell backdoor vulnerability discovered using Nessus Essentials.

As the student’s report showed, Claude’s approach — disabling the ingreslock entry in /etc/inetd.conf and de-registering the xinetd super-server — permanently removed the vulnerability at its source and survived reboots. ChatGPT’s suggestion to kill the process was effective in the moment but non-persistent. Gemini’s firewall rule blocked external access but left the backdoor process running locally. The student chose Claude’s method because it satisfied NIST SP 800-53 SI-2 requirements.

This kind of critical AI literacy — knowing not just how to use AI tools but how to evaluate and challenge their outputs — is precisely what the cybersecurity industry needs from the next generation of practitioners.

“Students discovered that different AI tools gave meaningfully different answers — not just in wording, but in technical depth, persistence, and correctness.”

Step 3: Microlearning Before Every Lab

Supporting both the Nessus work and the AI comparison tasks was a restructured content delivery model. Rather than front-loading a two-hour lecture, I broke module content into focused microlearning units of five to ten minutes each — delivered on MOVE, Majan’s e-learning platform, before each lab session.

Each unit was deliberately brief and focused, ensuring students arrived at labs already familiar with the core concept — meaning lab time could be spent entirely on application rather than explanation. A microlearning certificate upload task on MOVE reinforced completion and accountability without adding administrative burden.

At Majan University College, where many students balance studies with work and family responsibilities, the flexibility of microlearning also reduced cognitive overload. Bite-sized content reviewable on a phone during a commute proved far more accessible than dense lecture recordings.

What the Results Showed

After one full semester using this combined approach, the outcomes were encouraging. Student performance on practical assessments — particularly those requiring live vulnerability identification and remediation — improved noticeably compared to previous cohorts. Student feedback consistently highlighted increased confidence in applying tools independently, and the forum posts demonstrated a level of critical analytical writing that prior cohorts had rarely produced.

Several students who had previously struggled with abstract networking concepts were among the most engaged contributors to the AI comparison discussions. The practical, tool-driven format appeared to level the playing field in ways that traditional assessment had not.

Three Takeaways for Fellow Educators

1. Start with Nessus Essentials. Tenable offers free licences for students and educators. Having students scan their own machines creates an immediate, personal connection to the vulnerability concepts you are teaching.

2. Make AI comparison the assessment, not AI use. Asking students to compare three AI tools’ outputs builds critical thinking and AI literacy simultaneously — far more valuable than letting them use a single tool uncritically.

3. Keep microlearning units under ten minutes and single-topic. Pair each unit with a concrete lab task so the knowledge is applied within the same session it is introduced.

Cybersecurity education is no longer just about teaching student’s what threats exist. It is about equipping them to think like defenders in a world where the threats change faster than the textbooks — and where AI tools are both an asset and a variable that must itself be critically evaluated. What began as an experiment at Majan University College has become the foundation of how I approach every cybersecurity module I teach.

This is an abridged version of the full peer-reviewed article: A Pedagogical Framework for Embedding Microlearning, Gamification, and Industry Credentials in Undergraduate Cybersecurity Education — Ramalingam Dharmalingam, Majan University College, Muscat, Sultanate of Oman.
